story_text.value:
hi everyone, been building this project for the last ~1.5 months (cc+superpowers all the way)

it is an open effort to find a program that can reliably win NetHack 3.6.6: you can write a bot by hand, let claude code / codex / opencode improve one, or build your own harness that improves the thing that improves the bot

me and my lab switched to the goal-based research this year (we worked a lot in the idea-based framework for a last couple of years) -- and decided that we would like to tackle the NetHack, it is one of those nasty roguelike that is still somehow not solved with all fancy AI models (yes, even astra) -- probably on the way something useful will appear

you can pull someone else's bot, run experiments locally and register the results. every registered program is linked to your github repo and exact source commit

i always wanted to try building something that will use github as both social and storage layer (and it seems to work quite well in our case, simplified things a bit and i think this approach is quite cool)

there is a shared frontier across 73 starting identities -- your bots dont have to be the best at everything to contribute something useful, e.g. if you love to roleplay gnomes only, so be it

to make thing easier (for both harness devs and people who are just playing around), we provide a loop that does some sort of an evolutionary optimization process (quality-diversity, etc), ofc you don't have to use it. but you can start with in minutes (given you have codex or claude subs)

you can also bring your own search, your own harness, whatever -- the common ground is the evaluation. public seeds are there for people to overfit (in nethack even overfitting is hard), and we separately re-evaluate on hidden seeds to check whether the improvements actually transfer

one of my goals was to actually try to make it at least a bit fun -- hope you enjoy the web-site and easter eggs

story_text.value:
I've really enjoyed and am quite proud on where this project has become. I started this 6 years ago and it's gone through many iterations to get to this point. This latest iteration of what you see if you click and view the page has been roughly 6 months of development and testing and tweaking. I recently had an overhaul to the graphics and UX so I considered that as something valid to share again with you all.

The tech stack is react, with tailwindcss and hosted on cloudflare. I learned a whole lot about page speed and optimization, because it was just about a month ago I got feedback that the website was slow- my FCP was 34 seconds on mobile! This time around it isn't my first rodeo, and I was able to learn some tricks like font subsetting, dynamic javascript imports, setting explicit heights/widths of images to prevent content shifts, among other things in order to get my page speed in the mid 90's. This may be old knowledge if you've done this before, but it's been a good journey and I'm using this project not only for my own purposes, but also to grow and learn more about pieces of web development I never considered before.

It's not AI, and it's been a labor of love.

story_text.value:
Hey HN!

Owner of a first generation Logitech MX Master [1] and MX Keys S here, frequently switching between two Macs. Every time the mouse has to be turned over to access the button at the bottom, and keyboard has to be switched on it's own.

Logitech finally released an Options+ feature [2, 3] to switch multiple peripherals at the same time, with a single key press. The only problem - my ol' reliable isn't supported. It's a Unifying device, and only Bolt is officially supported. [4]

So, I made a fix - The Mouse Is Coming Too. There are 3 mini-apps, each coresponding to a different host device. Running any of them will switch both the mouse and the keyboard to a given host. They are mappable to "Open application" in Options+, so a programmable key can be used to trigger them.

Tested with MX Master and MX Keys S, but should work with any models recognised by Options+

[1] v1, bough some 9 years ago, and released in 2025. Still going strong after some ~9 years, micro-USB to USB-C conversion, skates replacement, stuck thumb button [5], and more than a few falls

[2] Yes, I should switch to something better

[3] https://marketplace.logi.com/releasenotes/optionsplus/en#2.6...

[4] To make it a bit more absurd, "easy switch" for this mouse already exists and works, but is accessible only through Options+ Action ring. Tried giving it a fair chance, but it's too cumbersome.

[5] https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3WNP1mnZx58

title.value: Show HN: The Mouse Is Coming Too – Easy Switch for Legacy Logitech Devices

story_text.value:
Hi HN,

I just open sourced the DSL that our harness in grep.ai uses to turn repeatable parts of agent work into workflows. You can combine tool calls, code, Jev-powered system one decisions for things like routing and screening evidence, and agents when a step needs more investigation.

Our harness uses the traces and retro notes agents leave behind when doing a job to figure out which parts can become a workflow. The idea is to make the work easier to understand and avoid paying for a full agent loop where one isn’t needed. For example, a research workflow can split a question into subquestions, send agents to research them in parallel, use Jev to screen the evidence, and have another agent write the report. You can inspect the steps, evaluate the evidence screening separately, or change one agent without rebuilding everything.

The DSL and examples are in our GitHub. There’s a scripted demo you can run without API keys: https://github.com/Parcha-ai/agentrun

You can also use it as a Pi extension to build, inspect, and run workflows: https://github.com/Parcha-ai/agentrun#use-it-in-pi

I would love to hear if this is useful to others.

More background on how AgentRun works in this video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vOVhtGjtwpg. Or read about our use cases in this article: https://x.com/MiguelriosEN/status/2101029313906987422.

story_text.value:
I'm travelling a lot, and often need to call numbers in my home country (a telco, a bank). Surprisingly, ever since Skype died, the apps that were meant to replace it launched once and never updated

So today, I'm presenting to you - Suparelay.

It works just like your phone... (revolutionary I know): - it remembers numbers you called - it looks like... a typical phone screen - it has a keypad that works during the call, for those "press 1 for your account" menus - it costs 90% less than using your local carrier for international calls

I compared 31 popular international calling destinations (in the Americas, Europe, Asia, Africa and Oceania) against 6 legacy carriers (T-Mobile US, AT&T Prepaid US, Vodafone UK, Airtel India, Claro Brazil and China Mobile), and to my surprise, the difference is insane.

Calls start from 2 cents a minute, you pay only when somebody answers, and there is no app to install: your browser is your phone.

Try it out and tell me what you think.

Say bye to vibe-coded Skype replacements, say hi to Suparelay!

title.value: Show HN: Suparelay – Call any phone in the world from a browser tab

story_text.value:
I built Ceptile because I wanted a search tool that could combine the convenience of an AI answer with the ability to inspect the actual web pages behind it. A Ceptile search retrieves pages from the web, ranks the retrieved sources, and uses them to produce an answer with links back to the sources. You can open the sources and continue researching from there.

I've also been building some things around the search workflow, including Notes for keeping research, translation tools, and ways to work with information found during a search. Just select a text in answer or web results, and it will show a toolbar to save it to notes, translate, etc.

The project is still early. A lot of the work so far has been figuring out the search pipeline itself: retrieving useful pages, dealing with noisy results, deciding which sources should be used, and keeping the connection between an answer and its sources.

I'm particularly interested in where the current system breaks down. For example, if you try it with a query that you already know well, I'd be interested in whether the retrieved sources are useful and whether the citations make it easy to verify the answer.

https://ceptile.com/

Watch 2 minutes demo on Youtube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OR4WfsMKEiE

Join Our Discord Server on: https://discord.gg/N9wRwBTDD

story_text.value:
Hello HN!

I've spent years debugging Windows crashes with tools that were either friendly but limited (e.g. Visual Studio) or powerful but archaic (e.g. WinDbg). I developed patterns and methods for understanding what was going on, and decided to build it into a much more effective debugging tool called ForensicDbg.

I built a modern interface to minimize the friction when debugging. All of the data shown to you is analyzed, interpreted, and presented to you clearly, so you can focus on what matters. Everything is interlinked so you can quickly and intuitivly navigate through the process space.

ForensicDbg comes with an MCP server which allows for agenic debugging. The work done to interpret and interlink your data also benefits AI tools. It removes the risk of hallucinations while building a stable foundation for them to work from without spending tokens.

If you want to try it out you can sign up and get a free beta license here: https://www.forensicdbg.com/beta
